Three forms of intellectual development

The development of modern Gujarati intellectual life can be understood through three related activities: the organisation of literary institutions, the publication of journals and the expansion of public libraries.

Literary institutions encourage writers, organise intellectual activities, preserve literary traditions and support publication. Journals communicate literary works, knowledge and public ideas to readers at regular intervals. Public libraries make reading material available to a wider population.

These activities complement each other. Literary institutions encourage the production of knowledge, journals circulate it, and public libraries broaden access to it.

Literary institutions and their publications

InstitutionEstablishedPrincipal associationPublication
Gujarat Vernacular Society1848Alexander Kinloch ForbesBuddhiprakash
Gujarati Sahitya Parishad1905Ranjitram MehtaParab
Gujarat Sahitya Akademi1981Government of GujaratShabdasrushti

Gujarat Vernacular Society was renamed Gujarat Vidya Sabha in 1946. Gujarati Sahitya Parishad developed as a literary association, whereas Gujarat Sahitya Akademi originated through a State Government initiative and became operational in 1982.

Comparison of the principal journals

JournalImportant datesPrincipal personalitiesDistinctive emphasis
Buddhiprakash1850; 1854Dalpatram, from 1855Knowledge, education and reform
Navjivan1915; 1919Indulal Yagnik and Mahatma GandhiNational awakening and Gandhian ideas
Kumar1924Ravishankar Raval and Bachubhai RawatLiterature, art and cultural education

The dates associated with Buddhiprakash and Navjivan require particular attention. Buddhiprakash first appeared as a fortnightly in 1850 and was revived as a monthly in 1854. Navjivan ane Satya began as a monthly in 1915, while Gandhi's Navjivan appeared as a weekly from 7 September 1919.

Baroda library movement

Sayajirao Gaekwad III provided the royal and administrative support for the public library system. W. A. Borden assisted in organising the system professionally from 1910. Motibhai Amin contributed to the expansion of village libraries and the development of mobile library services in 1911.

Motibhai Amin's earlier initiatives included the student library at Vaso in 1890 and Mitramandal Pustakalay at Petlad in 1906.

Chronological understanding

The Gujarat Vernacular Society and Buddhiprakash belong to the early phase of organised Gujarati literary and educational reform. The Gujarati Sahitya Parishad and Baroda library movement developed during the early 20th century. Navjivan and Kumar represent important developments in Gujarati journalism during the following decades. Gujarat Sahitya Akademi represents the later development of state-supported literary promotion after independence.

Avoid confusing historical roles

  • Forbes founded the Gujarat Vernacular Society; Dalpatram was its important literary associate and an editor of Buddhiprakash.
  • Ranjitram Mehta founded the Gujarati Sahitya Parishad; Govardhanram Tripathi presided over its first conference in 1905.
  • Indulal Yagnik started Navjivan ane Satya; Gandhi took over the publication in 1919.
  • Ravishankar Raval founded Kumar; Bachubhai Rawat was an important collaborator and later editor.
  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III sponsored the Baroda library system; Borden organised it professionally, and Motibhai Amin helped extend its rural reach.

[References: Hiralal T. Parekh, Gujarat Vernacular Societyno Itihas, Part 1, 1932, Chapters 3 and 15; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat Vidya Sabha, Gujarat Sahitya Akademi, Shabdasrushti and Kumar; Gujarati Sahitya Parishad, official History section; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Navajivan, Vol. 1, Issue 1, 7 September 1919; Ramesh Malabhai Chauhan, Gujarat's First Educational Conference: A Study, Towards Excellence, June 2021, p. 700; INFLIBNET Centre, Public Libraries, Pioneers of Public Library Movement in India: Part 1, sections 1–3. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
